fieldApplications.original: The cisternal segment hugs the committed `ctx-midbrain-surface` envelope (the same surface the three SCA courses declare): its middle waypoint is a literal vertex of it, 0.000 au from the surface. The TERMINAL is the opposite relation — a choroidal artery ends ON the plexus — so it is a deliberate graze on the committed `ctx-choroid-plexus-l` mesh (a literal plexus vertex), 12.664 au (15.20 mm) from the P2 take-off, which is the cisternal + choroidal-fissure interval the path crosses.

Source-backed placement is required; the retained waypoints and construction distances do not validate arterial anatomy.
fieldApplications.applied: Spatial route withheld. The former lateral-ventricular plexus endpoint does not establish a medial posterior choroidal course to the third-ventricular tela choroidea. Source-backed placement is required; the retained waypoints and construction distances do not validate arterial anatomy.

fieldApplications.original: Ia muscle-spindle and periodontal afferents of CN V that bypass the trigeminal ganglion and descend via the mesencephalic tract
fieldApplications.applied: Peripheral processes of mesencephalic trigeminal primary sensory neurons carry jaw-muscle-spindle and periodontal input through CN V; their cell bodies lie in the CNS rather than the trigeminal ganglion.

fieldApplications.original: Relay of the lateral (cerebellar) motor system in the rostral midbrain tegmentum. The caudal magnocellular part is the origin of the rubrospinal tract, which crosses immediately in the ventral tegmentum and facilitates flexor tone of the contralateral limbs; the rostral parvocellular part links the cerebellum with the inferior olive through the central tegmental tract (rubro-olivary, Guillain-Mollaret loop) and subserves motor learning. In humans the rubrospinal system is vestigial relative to the corticospinal tract, but the nucleus remains a major dentatorubrothalamic relay.
fieldApplications.applied: Motor-related nucleus of the rostral midbrain tegmentum. Its caudal magnocellular division gives rise to the crossed rubrospinal pathway, much less developed in humans than in many other mammals. Its rostral parvocellular division receives cerebellar and cortical inputs and projects to the ipsilateral inferior olive through the central tegmental tract. Cerebellothalamic fibers also pass through or around the red-nucleus region en route to the thalamus; these differ from fibers terminating in the red nucleus.

fieldApplications.original: Composite fiber systems of the basis pontis: the longitudinal fasciculi carry corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticopontine axons from the crus cerebri down to the medulla, while the transverse fibers arise from the pontine nuclei, decussate, and collect laterally as the middle cerebellar peduncle.
fieldApplications.applied: Composite fiber systems of the basis pontis: longitudinal fasciculi contain corticospinal axons continuing toward the medulla, corticobulbar axons reaching their brainstem targets, and corticopontine axons terminating in the pontine nuclei. Transverse pontocerebellar fibers arise from pontine neurons, cross the midline, and collect laterally as the middle cerebellar peduncle.

fieldApplications.original: Medial crus infarction with CN III fascicles: ipsilateral pupil-involving CN III palsy plus contralateral face-arm-leg hemiplegia.
fieldApplications.applied: A medial cerebral-peduncle lesion involving CN III fascicles can cause ipsilateral third-nerve palsy with contralateral motor weakness (Weber pattern); completeness, pupil involvement, and weakness distribution or severity depend on lesion extent.

fieldApplications.original: A lesion at the facial colliculus damages the abducens nucleus and the looping facial fibers together — ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy plus complete LMN facial paralysis (Foville syndrome), with loss of the ipsilateral blink.
fieldApplications.applied: A focal lesion involving the abducens nucleus and looping facial fibers can cause ipsilateral horizontal conjugate gaze palsy and lower motor neuron facial weakness, including impaired eyelid closure. The full classic Foville pattern adds contralateral body weakness when descending motor pathways are also involved; focal dorsal lesions need not include that component.

fieldApplications.original: AICA (caudal) and SCA (rostral) short circumferential branches of the basilar artery
fieldApplications.applied: Predominantly AICA branches, with SCA contributions and variable territorial overlap or anastomoses.

fieldApplications.original: Transsynaptic degeneration of the olive after a lesion of the Guillain-Mollaret triangle (dentate nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle, or central tegmental tract), producing palatal (palatopharyngeal) myoclonus/tremor months after the index lesion.
fieldApplications.applied: Disruption of afferent dentato-olivary pathways, such as dentate/superior cerebellar peduncle or central tegmental tract injury, can cause transsynaptic olivary degeneration. Delayed palatal or oculopalatal tremor may develop, but is not present in every case.

fieldApplications.original: MRI shows T2 hyperintensity with enlargement of the olive (hypertrophic degeneration, not atrophy).
fieldApplications.applied: MRI findings evolve with time: T2 hyperintensity may precede visible olivary enlargement, enlargement may develop later and then resolve, and signal abnormality may persist. Olivary size is not enlarged at every stage.

fieldApplications.original: PCA — tuberothalamic artery
fieldApplications.applied: Tuberothalamic (polar) artery, usually from the posterior communicating artery; paramedian PCA supply may substitute when the polar artery is absent.

fieldApplications.original: Acute anterograde amnesia, apathy, abulia and executive dysfunction; left-sided lesions add an 'aphasia-plus' state and right-sided lesions neglect, because the Papez circuit is interrupted at the anterior nucleus.
fieldApplications.applied: Anterior/tuberothalamic territory infarction can cause impaired new learning, apathy or abulia, and executive or orientation difficulties. Dominant-side lesions may affect language and nondominant-side lesions visuospatial attention; these depend on the nuclei and pathways involved and are not attributable to the anterior nucleus alone.

fieldApplications.original: Thiamine deficiency damages the anterior thalamic nuclei together with the mammillary bodies, producing dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation.
fieldApplications.applied: Thiamine-deficiency injury can involve mammillary bodies and thalamic/periventricular memory networks, including anterior and medial thalamus. Persistent Korsakoff amnesia may severely impair new learning; confabulation can occur and is variable.

fieldApplications.original: Obligatory relay of retinal vision to cortex: six layers receive a strictly retinotopic, eye-segregated map (ipsilateral eye 2/3/5, contralateral 1/4/6), with magnocellular layers serving motion and parvocellular layers form and color, forwarded to V1 via the retrolenticular internal capsule. Pupil-light-reflex fibers leave the optic tract before the LGN, so LGN lesions spare the light reflex.
fieldApplications.applied: Principal relay of the geniculostriate visual pathway to primary visual cortex: six layers receive a strictly retinotopic, eye-segregated map (ipsilateral eye 2/3/5, contralateral 1/4/6), with magnocellular layers serving motion and parvocellular layers form and color, forwarded to V1 via the retrolenticular internal capsule. Pupil-light-reflex fibers leave the optic tract before the LGN, so an isolated LGN lesion can spare the light reflex. Other retinal projections, including superior-collicular/pulvinar pathways, do not require the LGN as their relay.

fieldApplications.original: Rhythm and stress-coordination nucleus linking the suprachiasmatic clock to feeding and sleep-wake cycles: DMH neurons generate anticipatory locomotor and feeding rhythms and recruit endocrine (paraventricular) and autonomic outputs during stress.
fieldApplications.applied: Hypothalamic nucleus participating in circadian, feeding, stress, endocrine, and autonomic networks. Animal studies implicate DMH circuits in coordinating sleep-wake/physiological outputs and modulating meal anticipation; they do not establish a necessary food-anticipatory rhythm generator in humans.

fieldApplications.original: Myelinated limbic afferent bundle sweeping along the dorsomedial border of the thalamus from the septal/preoptic region to the habenular nuclei — the principal input limb of the epithalamic circuit feeding the anti-reward system.
fieldApplications.applied: Limbic afferent bundle running along the dorsomedial thalamic border from septal, preoptic, basal-forebrain, and hypothalamic regions to the habenular complex. Medial and lateral habenular circuits have distinct inputs and outputs; the entire bundle is not a single anti-reward pathway.

fieldApplications.original: Superior hypophyseal and anterior communicating branches superiorly; internal carotid and posterior communicating branches inferiorly (segmental supply underlies chiasmal infarction).
fieldApplications.applied: Variable contributions from superior hypophyseal, posterior communicating, anterior cerebral, and anterior communicating branches. Human dissections show important inferior pial supply from superior hypophyseal and posterior communicating arteries, with superior pial contributions and territorial overlap.

fieldApplications.original: Germinomas and pineal parenchymal tumors compress the pretectal plate and aqueduct — upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation, lid retraction, convergence-retraction nystagmus (Parinaud syndrome) with hydrocephalus; see the syndrome browser entry.
fieldApplications.applied: Germinomas and pineal parenchymal tumors may compress dorsal midbrain and/or cerebral aqueduct. Dorsal involvement can produce some combination of upgaze paresis, light-near dissociation, lid retraction, and convergence-retraction nystagmus (Parinaud pattern); aqueduct obstruction can cause hydrocephalus. Findings depend on tumor extent.

fieldApplications.original: Masses at the posterior third ventricle obstruct the cerebral aqueduct, causing headache, papilledema and gait failure before focal signs.
fieldApplications.applied: A mass near the posterior third ventricle may obstruct the cerebral aqueduct, causing hydrocephalus with headache, nausea/vomiting, papilledema, or other raised-pressure findings. Ocular motor or other focal signs may coexist; no fixed symptom order is established.

fieldApplications.original: Fastigial or vermal lesions give a wide-based staggering gait with truncal instability and nystagmus while limb coordination on the bed may be preserved; bilateral posterior fossa lesions therefore present predominantly as gait ataxia.
fieldApplications.applied: Medial cerebellar/fastigial and vestibular circuit lesions can cause truncal or gait instability and ocular motor abnormalities, with limb coordination relatively spared when hemispheric pathways are preserved. Intermediate/lateral circuit extension can add limb ataxia; bilateral posterior-fossa location alone does not define a predominantly gait syndrome.

fieldApplications.original: Small posterior-limb/genu infarcts give contralateral face-arm-leg weakness without cortical signs; larger capsular strokes add dense hemisensory loss and dysarthria-clumsy-hand syndrome.
fieldApplications.applied: Small posterior-limb or genu infarcts can cause contralateral weakness or dysarthria without cortical signs. Sensory loss, ataxic hemiparesis, or dysarthria-clumsy hand depend on involved pathways; dysarthria-clumsy hand itself can be a lacunar capsular syndrome.

fieldApplications.original: Contralateral incongruous homonymous hemianopia from anterior-choroidal-territory infarction of the optic radiations.
fieldApplications.applied: Retrolenticular optic-radiation injury can cause contralateral homonymous visual-field loss. Completeness and congruity depend on affected fibers and lesion extent; incongruity is not obligatory. Vascular supply is variable.

fieldApplications.original: Progressive caudate volume loss underlies chorea and frontal-executive decline — visible on the coronal context silhouettes.
fieldApplications.applied: Huntington disease involves progressive striatal degeneration, including caudate and putamen, with motor, cognitive, and behavioral manifestations and additional brain involvement. Caudate atrophy may be evident on patient CT or MRI; the invariant atlas silhouette does not demonstrate disease-related volume loss.
